headline: Fans Are Rebuilding Classic Video Games to Run Almost Anywhere

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: Some video game fans love old games so much that they rebuild them from scratch using computer code. This is called a 'decompile' or 'recompile.' It means they study how an old game works and then make a new version of it that can run on modern computers, phones, or even web browsers. For example, people made a way to play the classic game Halo right inside a web browser, with friends joining in too. Another group rebuilt a racing game called Lego Racers so it works on phones, computers, and browsers. Someone even got a game called Half-Life: Alyx working on a brand new type of headset called Vision Pro. These projects are not made by the companies who originally made the games, like Nintendo. Because of this, some people worry it might not be totally allowed. Still, fans keep doing it because they love these old games and want to keep playing them in new ways.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Video games from many years ago were built using special code that only worked on specific gaming systems, like old Nintendo consoles. Now, dedicated fans have found ways to take apart that old code, understand exactly how it works, and rebuild the games so they run on brand-new devices. This process is called decompiling or recompiling. Thanks to this work, people can now play Halo through a regular web browser with friends online, enjoy a Lego Racers game on phones and computers, and even play Half-Life: Alyx on a high-tech headset called Vision Pro. One writer shared how she now plays her favorite childhood game, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, using a fan-made version for computers instead of her old game disc. These projects let classic games survive even after old hardware breaks down or becomes hard to find. However, there's a catch: these are unofficial versions, not made or approved by the original companies. Big companies like Nintendo might not be thrilled that people are playing their games in ways they never intended, which puts these projects in a legally unclear area. Some of this work is also done with help from artificial intelligence, which upsets people who have concerns about AI's ethics or its impact on the environment. Even with these concerns, fans see this as a creative way to preserve gaming history and share it with new generations in exciting new formats.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: A growing movement among video game fans is transforming how classic games are played. Using a technique called decompiling, skilled programmers study the original code of old games and rebuild it piece by piece into a readable format. From there, they can 'recompile' the game so it runs on completely different devices than it was originally designed for. This has led to incredible results: Halo can now be played inside a web browser with online multiplayer, a 1999 Lego Racers game has been rebuilt to run on browsers, phones, and computers, and Half-Life: Alyx, a game built for virtual reality headsets, now works on Apple's Vision Pro headset. One journalist described replaying The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, a game she grew up with, through a fan-made PC port called Ship of Harkinian instead of digging out her old GameCube. These projects matter because they keep beloved games alive and accessible long after the original hardware becomes outdated, broken, or hard to find. They also let creative fans experiment, sometimes adding wild new features that were never part of the original design, like skateboarding inside a Call of Duty game. However, this hobby exists in murky legal territory. The companies that originally made these games, such as Nintendo, never approved these unofficial versions, and they could argue their copyrights are being violated. It's unclear whether these projects could someday face legal consequences, even though many fans see them as acts of love rather than theft. Adding to the controversy, some of these recreations are built with help from artificial intelligence tools. This bothers people who have ethical concerns about AI, such as worries over how AI models are trained or the large amount of energy they consume. Despite these unresolved questions, the decompilation community continues to grow, driven by passionate fans determined to preserve and reimagine gaming history for new generations and new technology.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: A fascinating trend is reshaping how people experience classic video games: fans are 'decompiling' and 'recompiling' old titles to free them from their original hardware. Decompiling means taking a game's compiled code—the machine-readable instructions a computer uses to run software—and reverse-engineering it back into a more human-readable form. Programmers can then rebuild, or recompile, that code so the game runs on entirely new platforms. The results are striking. Halo, once exclusive to specific consoles, now runs inside a standard web browser with full online multiplayer. A beloved 1999 racing game, Lego Racers, has been recreated as a browser-based title playable on desktop or phone, complete with split-screen and online features. Half-Life: Alyx, a game designed specifically for virtual reality systems, has been adapted to run natively on Apple's Vision Pro headset. Perhaps most emotionally resonant is the story of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, a game many players grew up with. Rather than relying on an aging GameCube disc, fans can now play it through Ship of Harkinian, an unofficial PC port built by an online community of hobbyist programmers. These projects highlight both the creative passion of gaming communities and the practical challenges of preserving digital history. As original hardware ages, breaks, or becomes prohibitively expensive, decompilation offers a way to keep beloved games playable indefinitely, independent of the devices they were originally built for. Some fans go further, using recompiled code as a foundation for wild modifications, like adding skateboarding mechanics to a Call of Duty game. However, this entire movement exists in a legally uncertain space. These are unofficial, unauthorized ports, meaning the original rights holders—companies like Nintendo—never approved them. It's reasonable to assume companies aren't thrilled to see their intellectual property running on competitors' hardware or modified in unexpected ways, raising real questions about whether these projects infringe on copyright law, even if no official legal action has been taken yet. Adding another layer of controversy, many decompilation efforts now incorporate artificial intelligence tools to speed up the painstaking process of analyzing old code. This use of AI troubles some observers who have broader concerns about the technology's ethical implications, including how AI models are trained on existing data, or its environmental costs, such as the significant energy and water consumption required to run large computing systems. Despite the unresolved legal and ethical questions, the decompilation community continues expanding rapidly, driven by a genuine desire to preserve gaming history and share it in innovative new ways with future generations of players.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: An unusual and increasingly influential movement is transforming the preservation and accessibility of classic video games: communities of hobbyist programmers are decompiling and recompiling old titles, effectively liberating them from the proprietary code and specific hardware for which they were originally designed. Decompilation is a technical process in which programmers take a game's compiled binary code—the low-level instructions a machine executes—and reverse-engineer it into a more readable, editable format, essentially reconstructing something close to the original source code. From there, developers can recompile this reconstructed code to run on entirely different systems, platforms, or operating environments than the game was initially built for. The practical results of this movement are remarkable. Halo, once tied to specific consoles, can now be played directly within a web browser, complete with functioning online multiplayer. Lego Racers, a 1999 kart-racing game, has been faithfully recreated by a fan developer as a browser-based title playable across desktop and mobile devices, supporting both split-screen and online multiplayer modes, with additional builds available for Windows, Mac, Linux, and the Steam Deck. Half-Life: Alyx, originally designed exclusively for virtual reality systems, has reportedly been adapted to run natively on Apple's Vision Pro headset, a device released years after the game's original launch. Perhaps the most personally resonant example involves The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. One journalist described her long-standing emotional connection to the game, which she had traditionally revisited by dusting off an aging GameCube and hoping its disc still functioned. Thanks to Ship of Harkinian, an unofficial PC port built collaboratively by an online community, she can now experience the game without relying on deteriorating original hardware at all. These developments carry genuine significance beyond mere nostalgia. As gaming consoles age, become obsolete, or simply break down, decompilation offers a pathway toward long-term digital preservation, ensuring that culturally significant games remain playable regardless of the fate of their original hardware. It also empowers fan creativity in unprecedented ways, enabling radical modifications, such as integrating skateboarding mechanics into a Call of Duty title, that would never receive official sanction from the original publisher. Nevertheless, this entire ecosystem operates within a legally ambiguous gray zone. These projects are unauthorized by the original rights holders, meaning companies such as Nintendo have not sanctioned the use of their intellectual property on non-Nintendo hardware. It is reasonable to infer that such companies may object to their protected creative works being redistributed, modified, or ported without permission, raising unresolved questions under copyright law that could, in theory, result in legal challenges, even though enforcement has so far been inconsistent. Compounding this controversy, many decompilation projects increasingly rely on artificial intelligence tools to accelerate the labor-intensive process of translating low-level code into readable formats. This reliance alienates some community members and observers who hold ethical objections to AI technology, whether concerning the data used to train such models or the substantial environmental costs associated with the energy and computing resources AI systems demand. Despite these legal and ethical tensions remaining unresolved, the decompilation and recompilation community continues to grow, propelled by a sincere commitment among hobbyists to preserve gaming history and reimagine it for new technological contexts and future generations of players.

questions: If you could bring an old video game back to life on a new device, which game would you choose and why would it matter to you?
Do you think fans should be allowed to rebuild and share games without permission from the original companies? Why or why not?
How do you think using artificial intelligence to help rebuild old games might affect fairness, creativity, or the environment?
